rationale: A wins because it keeps the founder out of the ditch: its best angle, "Khan Academy's AI tutor reaches 1 million more students before the research is in," is framed around the real tension and demands the methodology before anyone pitches the learning claim. B has the same basic spine, but it gets sloppy where it cannot afford to, especially "districts are signing on to expand to 1 million students based on a study" — causality the update never gives. That is how a decent angle becomes a correction waiting to happen.
gaps_in_A: "A donor-funded nonprofit is giving away AI tutoring that competitors sell" asserts competitor behavior the update does not supply. The funding angle is good; that headline needs proof or a rewrite.
"The prevailing belief is that a nonprofit's free tool sidesteps the scrutiny applied to commercial edtech" is a plausible thesis, not a supplied fact. Don't smuggle punditry in as market reality.

"the pilot districts have a full stretch of classroom use behind them" overstates the record. The update says first classroom results from pilot districts, not duration, completeness, or breadth of classroom use.
gaps_in_B: "districts are signing on to expand to 1 million students based on a study" invents the districts' decision basis. The rollout and study are simultaneous; the update does not say the study drove adoption.
"While VC-backed EdTech companies charge districts" is imported market color. Maybe true, maybe not; either way it is not in the update.
"a body of research on productive failure and desirable difficulty argues" brings in an outside research frame as if it is already sourced. Useful proof to seek, not a fact to assert in the angle.

"The teacher angle is the most differentiated pitch in this set" is not backed by the actual material. It still needs named teachers, workload data, and task specifics before it is more than a feature idea.
